'''Philip Thaxton Gressman''' (born November 22, 1978) is an American [[mathematician]] and professor of mathematics at the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. His research is in [[harmonic analysis]], geometry, and partial differential equations, including work on geometric averaging operators, oscillatory integral operators, Fourier restriction, and the [[Boltzmann equation]]. He was named a [[:Category:Fellows of the American Mathematical Society|Fellow of the American Mathematical Society]] in the 2025 class.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ams.org/fellows_by_year.cgi?year=2025 |title=2025 Class of Fellows of the AMS |website=American Mathematical Society |access-date=2026-06-04}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Gressman grew up in [[Ava, Missouri]], and graduated from Ava High School in 1997.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://passporttoknowledge.com/lfm/discuss/9611/article-72.html |title=Mailing List WWW Gateway |website=Passport to Knowledge |access-date=2018-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020823034220/http://passporttoknowledge.com/lfm/discuss/9611/article-72.html |archive-date=2002-08-23 |url-status=live}}</ref> He received a Bachelor of Arts degree from [[Washington University in St. Louis]] in 2001, where he double majored in mathematics and physics, and was advised by [[Guido Weiss]] and Edward N. Wilson.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://math.wustl.edu/files/math/imce/newsletter16feb2009.pdf |title=Washington University Math Department Newsletter |date=2008 |access-date=2019-03-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190328234620/https://math.wustl.edu/files/math/imce/newsletter16feb2009.pdf |archive-date=2019-03-28 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
 |url=https://users.math.yale.edu/~pg245/
 |title=Philip Gressman
 |website=Yale University Department of Mathematics
 |access-date=2018-06-13
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150709103619/http://users.math.yale.edu/~pg245/
 |archive-date=2015-07-09
 |url-status=dead
}}</ref> He completed a PhD in mathematics at [[Princeton University]] in 2005 under the supervision of [[Elias Stein]]; his dissertation was titled ''Lp-Lq estimates for radon-like operators''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=89109 |title=Philip Gressman - Mathematics Genealogy Project |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=2018-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180809123604/https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=89109 |archive-date=2018-08-09 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
After completing his doctorate, Gressman was a J. W. Gibbs Assistant Professor at [[Yale University]] from 2005 to 2008.<ref name="shortcv">{{cite web |url=https://www.math.upenn.edu/~gressman/Gressman_CV_short.pdf |title=Philip T. Gressman Short Curriculum Vitae |website=Department of Mathematics, University of Pennsylvania |access-date=2018-07-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200604214637/https://www.math.upenn.edu/~gressman/Gressman_CV_short.pdf |archive-date=2020-06-04 |url-status=live}}</ref> He joined the faculty of the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 2008, where he serves as professor of mathematics and undergraduate chair.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.math.upenn.edu/people/philip-gressman |title=Philip Gressman |website=Department of Mathematics, University of Pennsylvania |access-date=2026-06-04}}</ref>

Gressman's research investigates the intersection of harmonic analysis and geometry. His areas of interest include geometric averaging operators, oscillatory integral operators, sublevel set estimates, Fourier restriction, and other problems in analysis and partial differential equations.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.math.upenn.edu/people/philip-gressman |title=Philip Gressman |website=Department of Mathematics, University of Pennsylvania |access-date=2026-06-04}}</ref>

He is known for his joint work with Robert M. Strain on the [[Boltzmann equation]]. Their work established existence, uniqueness, and rapid convergence to equilibrium for perturbative classical solutions of the Boltzmann equation with long-range interactions.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Global classical solutions of the Boltzmann equation without angular cut-off |first1=Philip T. |last1=Gressman |first2=Robert M. |last2=Strain |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |volume=24 |issue=3 |year=2011 |pages=771–847 |doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-2011-00697-8 |arxiv=1011.5441 |s2cid=115167686}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/university-pennsylvania-mathematicians-solve-140-year-old-boltzmann-equation-gaseous-behaviors |title=Mathematicians Solve 140-Year-Old Boltzmann Equation |website=Penn Today |date=2010-05-12 |access-date=2018-07-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180719054150/https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/university-pennsylvania-mathematicians-solve-140-year-old-boltzmann-equation-gaseous-behaviors |archive-date=2018-07-19 |url-status=live}}</ref>
